A real estate database uses an Object-Oriented approach: a Property object has attributes (address, price) and methods (calculateMortgage(), generateListing()). A ResidentialProperty class inherits all Property attributes but adds BedroomCount and GardenArea. Each object has a system-assigned unique OID.

Which OOP feature does the ResidentialProperty inheriting from Property demonstrate, and what is the OID's role?
opts: Encapsulation — OID stores data and methods together
Polymorphism — OID allows different responses to the same method call
Inheritance — ResidentialProperty reuses Property's attributes/behaviours; OID uniquely identifies each object regardless of attribute changes
Abstraction — OID hides implementation details from users
questions.explanation:
Inheritance allows new object classes to be defined based on existing classes — ResidentialProperty inherits from Property. An Object Identifier (OID) is assigned to each object to uniquely identify it regardless of changes to its attribute values (unlike primary keys which might change). OIDs simplify referencing and linking objects in a database.

{"A":"Encapsulation combines data and methods into one object — not what inheritance or OID represent.","B":"Polymorphism enables different objects to respond differently to the same method call — not demonstrated here.","C":"✓ Correct — child class using parent's attributes/methods = Inheritance; permanent object identifier = OID.","D":"Abstraction hides complexity — neither inheritance nor OID is specifically about abstraction."}

questions.text:
A recommendation engine is being designed for a streaming platform. It needs to answer: "Find all users who watched Movie A, identify movies those users also watched, find the top 5 most watched among those, and recommend them to User X if he hasn't watched them." This query involves traversing User → Watch → Movie → Rating relationships.

Which database type is most appropriate, and which graph algorithm best supports recommendation ranking?
opts: Relational Database — GROUP BY and ORDER BY for ranking
Graph Database — PageRank or similar centrality algorithm for influence-based ranking
Key-Value Store — fast lookup of precomputed recommendations
Column-Family Store — columnar aggregation of ratings
questions.explanation:
Recommendation Engines (suggesting content based on user behaviour and shared interests) are an explicit Graph Database use case. The traversal User→Watch→Movie→Rating is natural in a graph. PageRank measures the influence/importance of nodes — in a recommendation context, it identifies movies watched by many connected users. Graph algorithms like PageRank and community detection power modern recommendation systems.

{"A":"Relational DB with GROUP BY can rank — but multi-hop traversal across users and movies requires expensive JOIN chains.","B":"✓ Correct — graph traversal for recommendation + PageRank for ranking = Graph Database.","C":"Key-Value stores can cache precomputed results but cannot perform the traversal to generate recommendations.","D":"Column-family stores aggregate column data — not relationship-based recommendation traversal."}

questions.text:
A growing e-commerce startup finds that adding more RAM and CPU to its single database server is becoming prohibitively expensive. When they try to spread the database across multiple servers, the rigid table schema and complex foreign key constraints make the data very difficult to distribute cleanly.

Which traditional DBMS limitation does this scenario describe?
opts: High Maintenance Costs
Scalability Issues — vertical scaling hits limits and rigid schemas impede horizontal scaling
Security and Compliance Challenges
Limited Support for Real-Time Analytics
questions.explanation:
Scalability Issues: traditional DBMS (particularly relational databases) struggle with large volumes of data and concurrent transactions. Vertical scaling (adding more power to one machine) is costly with limits. Horizontal scaling (distributing across multiple servers) is challenging due to rigid schema structures (foreign keys, joins across nodes). Both aspects are demonstrated in this scenario.

{"A":"High Maintenance Costs relate to DBA staffing and operational overhead — not scaling architecture challenges.","B":"✓ Correct — expensive vertical scaling + rigid schema blocking horizontal distribution = scalability issues.","C":"Security challenges relate to encryption and compliance gaps — not scaling architecture.","D":"Real-time analytics limitations relate to OLAP vs OLTP performance — not infrastructure scaling costs."}

questions.text:
A social media company tries to store Instagram-style posts in its Oracle relational database. Posts have completely different structures: a video post has Duration and Thumbnail fields; a story has ExpiryTime; a reel has AudioTrack and Effects. The DBA has to run ALTER TABLE dozens of times as new post types emerge, breaking existing application queries each time.

Which traditional DBMS limitation is responsible for this operational pain?
opts: Concurrency and Locking Issues
Rigid Schema Design — predefined schemas require significant modification when data structures change
Limited Support for Cloud Integration
Inability to Handle Distributed Data
questions.explanation:
Rigid Schema Design: traditional DBMS require predefined schemas, meaning any change in data structure necessitates significant modifications. This rigidity makes it difficult to handle dynamic and unstructured data efficiently. Constantly running ALTER TABLE as new social media post types emerge — each breaking existing queries — is a direct consequence of rigid schema design.

{"A":"Concurrency issues cause deadlocks during simultaneous access — not structural inflexibility for varying data types.","B":"✓ Correct — needing ALTER TABLE for every new post type with different fields = rigid schema limitation.","C":"Cloud integration challenges relate to migration complexity — not schema inflexibility.","D":"Distributed data challenges relate to consistency across nodes — not schema change overhead."}

questions.text:
A financial services company's relational database performs well for daily transaction processing (OLTP). However, when the business intelligence team runs quarterly reports analysing 10 years of transaction history across 800 million records, queries take 14 hours — rendering them practically useless for business decisions.

Which traditional DBMS limitation does this exemplify?
opts: Security and Compliance Challenges
High Maintenance Costs
Rigid Schema Design
Limited Performance with Big Data — poor OLAP performance on massive structured datasets
questions.explanation:
Limited Performance with Big Data: the structured approach of traditional databases makes them inefficient for handling massive datasets. Also: traditional databases are optimised for OLTP but struggle with OLAP. Running complex analytical queries on 800 million historical records — taking 14 hours — illustrates both the big data performance limitation and the OLTP-vs-OLAP mismatch of traditional DBMS.

{"A":"Security challenges relate to encryption and compliance — not 14-hour analytical query performance.","B":"High maintenance costs relate to DBA staffing overhead — not query performance on large datasets.","C":"Rigid schema design relates to difficulty changing table structures — not analytical performance.","D":"✓ Correct — traditional DBMS optimised for OLTP; OLAP on 800M records taking 14 hours = limited big data performance."}

questions.text:
During a Black Friday sale, a retail bank's database experiences: 20,000 concurrent users attempting transactions, multiple timeouts as transactions queue behind locks, two incidents where Teller A and Teller B simultaneously tried to update the same customer balance causing the system to roll back one transaction, and significantly degraded response times across all branches.

Which traditional DBMS limitation is the primary cause of these problems?
opts: Scalability Issues
Concurrency and Locking Issues — concurrent transactions causing locks, deadlocks, and performance degradation
Rigid Schema Design
Limited Cloud Integration
questions.explanation:
Concurrency and Locking Issues: handling concurrent transactions can lead to locking and deadlocks, affecting performance and user experience. As multiple users access and modify data, contention for resources slows down transaction processing. Timeouts, rollbacks from simultaneous balance updates, and degraded response times are all classic symptoms of concurrency and locking problems.

{"A":"Scalability Issues relate to growing hardware costs and schema-based distribution challenges — deadlocks are a concurrency problem.","B":"✓ Correct — lock queues, deadlocks (simultaneous balance update), timeouts, and degraded performance = concurrency and locking issues.","C":"Rigid schema relates to structural inflexibility — not transaction conflict during simultaneous access.","D":"Cloud integration relates to migration complexity — not concurrent transaction management."}

questions.text:
A traditional DBMS vendor's sales pitch highlights: row-level locking, B-tree indexes, stored procedures, and triggers. A consultant responds: "All excellent for day-to-day transactions. But what about when your client needs to store IoT sensor JSON payloads with different fields for each device type? Or social media comment threads? Or graph-structured knowledge bases?"

Which limitation(s) is the consultant pointing to?
opts: High Maintenance Costs and Security Challenges
Inability to Handle NoSQL Requirements — unstructured/semi-structured data and non-relational models are beyond traditional RDBMS
Scalability Issues and Rigid Schema working together
Limited Performance with Big Data and Concurrency Issues
questions.explanation:
Inability to Handle NoSQL Requirements: many modern applications require NoSQL capabilities to manage unstructured or semi-structured data. Traditional relational databases are not designed to accommodate JSON payloads with varying fields (document store use case), social threads (flexible document/graph use case), or knowledge graphs (graph database use case). They are unsuitable for IoT, social media, and big data analytics — exactly what the consultant raises.

{"A":"Maintenance and security are real limitations but not what JSON payloads, social threads, or knowledge graphs represent.","B":"✓ Correct — IoT JSON, social comments, knowledge graphs = NoSQL-style unstructured/graph data = inability to handle NoSQL requirements.","C":"While schema rigidity overlaps, the consultant is specifically pointing to the NoSQL data model mismatch.","D":"Big data performance and concurrency are separate limitations from the NoSQL data model mismatch."}

questions.text:
A traditional bank wants to move its Oracle on-premises database to Google Cloud. The IT director reports: "The schema is so deeply coupled to on-premises infrastructure — fixed file paths, local networking assumptions, and hardware-specific storage configurations — that migration will take 18 months and cost ₦200 million."

Which traditional DBMS limitation explains this migration difficulty?
opts: Rigid Schema Design
High Maintenance Costs
Limited Support for Cloud Integration — traditional DBMS not optimised for cloud-native environments
Concurrency and Locking Issues
questions.explanation:
Limited Support for Cloud Integration: while cloud computing has become essential for modern businesses, traditional DBMS are often not optimised for cloud-native environments. Migrating legacy databases to the cloud can be complex, requiring extensive modifications and reconfiguration. The 18-month, ₦200M migration complexity directly reflects this limitation.

{"A":"Rigid schema relates to data structure inflexibility — not infrastructure coupling and cloud migration.","B":"High maintenance costs refer to ongoing DBA overhead — not one-time migration complexity.","C":"✓ Correct — traditional DBMS not cloud-native, causing complex expensive migration = limited cloud integration.","D":"Concurrency issues relate to simultaneous transaction management — not cloud migration."}

questions.text:
A hospital is told its traditional DBMS provides username/password access and AES-128 encryption, but the regulator requires: field-level encryption for patient identifiers, zero-trust network access policies, NDPR-compliant audit trails with tamper-proof logging, and automated right-to-erasure enforcement.

Which traditional DBMS limitation is the hospital facing?
opts: Scalability Issues
Rigid Schema Design
Security and Compliance Challenges — basic security mechanisms insufficient for modern regulatory requirements
Limited Performance with Big Data
questions.explanation:
Security and Compliance Challenges: traditional DBMS provide basic security (access control, encryption) but often lack robust support for modern needs — advanced encryption techniques (field-level), zero-trust architectures, and compliance with evolving regulations (GDPR, CCPA, NDPR). The gap between basic DBMS security and the regulator's requirements illustrates this limitation.

{"A":"Scalability Issues relate to data volume and horizontal distribution — not security architecture gaps.","B":"Rigid schema relates to structural inflexibility — not encryption standards or audit trail compliance.","C":"✓ Correct — basic security insufficient for field-level encryption, zero-trust, and regulatory compliance = security and compliance challenges.","D":"Big data performance relates to analytical query speed — not security and compliance architecture."}

questions.text:
A logistics company's DBA team of three spends: 40% of time on query tuning for degraded queries, 30% on backup and recovery management, 20% on security patching and user management, and 10% on capacity planning. The annual DBA cost is ₦45 million. The CFO asks why the database is so expensive to run.

Which traditional DBMS limitation does this cost structure reflect?
opts: Concurrency and Locking Issues
Rigid Schema Design
High Maintenance Costs — traditional DBMS require significant human and financial resources for ongoing operation
Limited Cloud Integration
questions.explanation:
High Maintenance Costs: managing a traditional DBMS requires significant resources — including database administrators for optimisation, security, and regular maintenance. This increases overall operational costs, especially for large enterprises. The ₦45M annual DBA cost covering query tuning, backup management, security patching, and capacity planning is a direct manifestation of high maintenance costs.

{"A":"Concurrency issues cause deadlocks — not recurring maintenance labour costs.","B":"Rigid schema causes structural inflexibility — not ongoing operational staffing costs.","C":"✓ Correct — significant DBA resources needed for ongoing optimisation, security, and maintenance = high maintenance costs.","D":"Cloud integration relates to migration difficulty — not recurring operational labour costs."}

questions.text:
A startup is choosing a database. Their data consists of: (a) structured user account records with fixed fields, (b) unstructured product reviews with varying fields, (c) social connection graphs between users, and (d) real-time click-stream events with timestamps. The CTO asks: "What is the single most important first factor to determine?"

Which database selection factor should the CTO evaluate first?
opts: Maintenance and Vendor Ecosystem — choose the database with the best support contracts
Data Model — what is the nature of the data and how will it be queried
Scalability — choose the system with the most horizontal scaling nodes
Performance — choose the system with the lowest latency benchmarks
questions.explanation:
The Data Model is described as "perhaps the most critical factor" in database selection — it determines how data is organised, stored, and queried. The CTO's data includes structured (RDBMS), unstructured/varied (NoSQL Document), social graph (Graph DB), and time-series (TSDB) — all requiring different models. Understanding the nature of each data type and its query patterns is the prerequisite for all other decisions.

{"A":"Maintenance and vendor ecosystem is a secondary consideration after the fundamental data model fit.","B":"✓ Correct — data model is the most critical first factor; it determines which database category is even viable.","C":"Scalability is important but secondary — you must first know the data model before choosing how to scale it.","D":"Performance benchmarks are meaningful only after the correct data model is identified."}

questions.text:
Company A chooses PostgreSQL and adds RAM and CPU to its single server as load grows (vertical scaling). Company B distributes its database across 50 cloud nodes, routing queries to the nearest node (horizontal scaling). Company A hits a hardware ceiling; Company B keeps scaling seamlessly.

Which database selection consideration does this comparison illustrate?
opts: Data Model — relational vs NoSQL
Workload Type — OLTP vs OLAP
Scalability — vertical scaling (scale-up) vs horizontal scaling (scale-out)
Consistency and Availability — CAP Theorem trade-offs
questions.explanation:
Scalability: vertical scaling (scale-up) involves upgrading server hardware — typical of traditional RDBMS — and hits physical/cost limits. Horizontal scaling (scale-out) distributes data across multiple servers — common in NoSQL and NewSQL. For applications expecting massive growth in user or transaction volume, horizontal scaling is preferable. This is the exact comparison illustrated.

{"A":"Data model relates to how data is structured — not the scaling architecture choice.","B":"OLTP vs OLAP relates to workload type (transactional vs analytical) — not horizontal vs vertical scaling.","C":"✓ Correct — Company A = vertical scaling hits ceiling; Company B = horizontal scaling = scalability consideration.","D":"CAP Theorem trade-offs relate to consistency/availability in distributed systems — not vertical vs horizontal scaling."}

questions.text:
A bank's payment system processes 15,000 financial transactions per second, each requiring a debit from one account and a credit to another — both must succeed or neither can. The system cannot tolerate inconsistent reads where one account appears debited but the other not yet credited.

Which database characteristic is NON-NEGOTIABLE for this payment system?
opts: Schema flexibility — different transaction types may need different fields
Eventual consistency — the system can tolerate temporary inconsistency for performance
ACID compliance — all-or-nothing transactions with consistent reads are mandatory
Horizontal NoSQL scaling — payment volume requires distributed NoSQL
questions.explanation:
ACID compliance is non-negotiable for financial payment systems. Atomicity ensures debit and credit both succeed or neither persists. Consistency ensures the database moves between valid states only. Isolation ensures concurrent transactions don't produce inconsistent intermediate states. Durability ensures committed transactions survive crashes. Eventual consistency would allow the exact error described (debit seen but credit not yet applied).

{"A":"Schema flexibility (NoSQL feature) is not relevant — payment transactions have fixed, well-defined structures.","B":"Eventual consistency explicitly allows temporary inconsistency — catastrophic for payment systems where half-transactions are visible.","C":"✓ Correct — payment debit/credit as atomic unit, no inconsistent reads = ACID compliance is mandatory.","D":"Some NoSQL systems lack full ACID — for payments, ACID is the requirement; NoSQL may or may not support it."}

questions.text:
A media company runs two separate workflows: (A) journalists adding news articles to the CMS (short, fast, frequent writes — 2,000 per hour); and (B) the analytics team aggregating 5 years of article data to model content performance trends (complex, slow, infrequent reads across 50 million records).

What workload type consideration does this scenario illustrate, and what is the implication for database selection?
opts: OLTP vs OLAP — workflow A is transactional (OLTP), workflow B is analytical (OLAP); they may need different optimised databases
Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling — workflow A needs horizontal, workflow B needs vertical
NoSQL vs SQL — workflow A needs NoSQL, workflow B needs SQL
CAP Theorem — workflow A prioritises availability, workflow B prioritises consistency
questions.explanation:
OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) handles high-volume, short transactional operations — workflow A (2,000 article inserts per hour). OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) handles complex queries on large datasets for BI and reporting — workflow B (5-year trend analysis on 50M records). Traditional DBMS are optimised for OLTP but struggle with OLAP. The implication: these may need different, purpose-optimised systems (e.g., PostgreSQL for OLTP, Apache Spark/BigQuery for OLAP).

{"A":"✓ Correct — frequent short writes = OLTP; complex long aggregations = OLAP; workload type determines database optimisation.","B":"Scaling direction (horizontal vs vertical) is not the primary distinction between these two workflows.","C":"Both could use SQL — the distinction is workload pattern (transactional vs analytical), not query language.","D":"CAP Theorem applies to distributed system consistency/availability — not the OLTP vs OLAP workload distinction."}

questions.text:
A hospital needs a database for its patient appointment system. The system will be accessed by 5 doctors at a single clinic, managing 200 appointments per day, with strict need for data accuracy (no double-bookings), and a fixed, well-defined data structure.

Which database type is most appropriate, and why?
opts: NoSQL Document Store — for schema flexibility
Distributed Database across 10 nodes — for scalability
Relational Database (RDBMS) — structured data, small scale, ACID requirements, well-defined schema
Time-Series Database — for time-stamped appointments
questions.explanation:
Choosing the right database requires matching the database to the specific needs: the data is structured (fixed schema), scale is small (5 doctors, 200 daily appointments), ACID compliance is required (no double-bookings = integrity), and the schema is well-defined. An RDBMS is ideal for structured, transactional, small-to-medium scale scenarios with fixed schemas. Over-engineering with distributed NoSQL or TSDB would be inappropriate.

{"A":"NoSQL Document stores are for schema flexibility with varied fields — appointments have a fixed structure.","B":"A 10-node distributed database is massive over-engineering for 5 doctors and 200 daily appointments.","C":"✓ Correct — structured, small scale, ACID needed, fixed schema = RDBMS is the appropriate choice.","D":"Time-Series databases handle high-frequency sensor/metric data — appointment scheduling is not a time-series problem."}

questions.text:
A startup CTO argues: "We should use a managed cloud database service — it reduces our operational burden even if it costs a bit more monthly." The CFO counters: "But we'd be completely dependent on one vendor and couldn't easily switch later."

Which database selection consideration does this disagreement reflect?
opts: Data Model selection — relational vs NoSQL
Maintenance and Vendor Ecosystem — managed services reduce maintenance but may create vendor lock-in
Scalability — the cloud has unlimited horizontal scaling
CAP Theorem — the cloud guarantees both consistency and availability
questions.explanation:
Maintenance and Vendor Ecosystem: managed cloud services (like Amazon RDS, Google BigQuery) reduce maintenance but may involve vendor lock-in. Open-source databases provide flexibility but require more in-house expertise. The CTO values reduced operational burden; the CFO is concerned about vendor lock-in — this is precisely the trade-off described in the database selection consideration of Maintenance and Vendor Ecosystem.

{"A":"Data model selection (relational vs NoSQL) is about data structure — not operational overhead vs vendor dependency.","B":"✓ Correct — managed services reduce maintenance but create vendor lock-in = Maintenance and Vendor Ecosystem trade-off.","C":"Horizontal scaling is one cloud benefit but not the subject of this specific CTO-CFO disagreement.","D":"CAP Theorem guarantees are per-database, not a blanket cloud promise — and not the subject of this discussion."}

questions.text:
A national statistics agency's DBMS was built in 2005 for centralised data storage. The agency now wants: real-time data feeds from 36 state offices simultaneously, replication to a disaster recovery site in Abuja, and a read replica for the Lagos analytics team. The system administrator says these requirements were "never part of the design."

Which traditional DBMS limitation is the administrator identifying?
opts: Security and Compliance Challenges
Rigid Schema Design
Complexity in Handling Distributed Data — traditional DBMS designed for centralised storage struggle with distributed requirements
Concurrency and Locking Issues
questions.explanation:
Complexity in Handling Distributed Data: traditional DBMS were designed for centralised data storage. As modern applications demand global accessibility and distributed data storage, traditional databases struggle with maintaining consistency, replication, and synchronisation across multiple locations. Real-time feeds from 36 offices, disaster recovery replication, and read replicas are distributed requirements that a centralised 2005 DBMS was never built to handle.

{"A":"Security challenges relate to encryption and compliance — not geographic distribution and replication.","B":"Rigid schema relates to structural inflexibility — not distribution and replication architecture.","C":"✓ Correct — centralised-only DBMS unable to handle multi-office replication and distributed reads = distributed data complexity.","D":"Concurrency issues relate to simultaneous transaction locking — not geographic distribution."}

questions.text:
A performance engineering team measures three metrics for a database candidate: (a) how quickly it responds to individual queries (latency), (b) how many operations it can handle per second (throughput), and (c) whether it continues operating correctly when one of its servers fails (fault tolerance).

Which database selection consideration do these three metrics collectively represent?
opts: Data Model — metrics define what type of data the database can store
Scalability — these metrics define how many nodes are needed
Performance Requirements — latency, throughput, and fault tolerance are performance criteria
Workload Type — OLTP requires low latency; OLAP requires high throughput
questions.explanation:
Performance Requirements: performance metrics such as latency (how quickly queries are answered), throughput (how many operations per second), and fault tolerance (ability to remain operational during failures) matter significantly. Applications requiring real-time data processing need low-latency, high-throughput, fault-tolerant systems. These three are explicitly listed as performance criteria in the database selection framework.

{"A":"Data model defines data structure organisation — not operational performance metrics.","B":"Scalability is about growing with user/data load — while related, the three specific metrics define performance requirements.","C":"✓ Correct — latency, throughput, and fault tolerance = the three performance requirements criteria.","D":"OLTP vs OLAP is the workload type consideration — performance requirements are a separate (though related) factor."}

questions.text:
An architect states: "No single database fits all scenarios." She designs a system using: PostgreSQL for customer and order records, Redis for real-time inventory caching, MongoDB for product catalogue with varying attributes, and InfluxDB for telemetry from delivery vehicles.

What database design strategy does the architect employ, and what principle justifies it?
opts: Database Consolidation — all data in one system for simplicity
Polyglot Persistence — using multiple purpose-fit databases, each chosen for its specific data domain and query pattern
ACID Enforcement — applying ACID to all four databases
Schema Standardisation — all four databases share a unified schema
questions.explanation:
"No single database fits all scenarios. The right choice depends on data characteristics, workload, scalability needs, consistency requirements, and operational capabilities." The architect uses each database for its strength: PostgreSQL (structured/transactional), Redis (speed/caching), MongoDB (flexible catalogue), InfluxDB (time-series telemetry). This deliberate multi-database strategy is called Polyglot Persistence.

{"A":"Consolidation merges everything into one system — opposite of the four-database strategy described.","B":"✓ Correct — different databases for different domains based on their strengths = Polyglot Persistence.","C":"ACID applies per-database — it is not a strategy for choosing which databases to use.","D":"Schema standardisation across different database types is not feasible — each database type has its own data model."}

questions.text:
The course material states: "Although traditional DBMS have been reliable for structured data management, their limitations have led to the rise of NoSQL, NewSQL, and other modern database technologies."

Which statement correctly summarises WHY modern database technologies emerged?
opts: Traditional DBMS were insecure and unreliable — modern databases fix all their bugs
Modern databases are always cheaper — organisations switched purely for cost reasons

Traditional DBMS limitations in scalability, schema flexibility, unstructured data handling, distributed computing, and real-time analytics drove demand for NoSQL, NewSQL, cloud-native, and specialised databases
NoSQL databases are strictly superior to traditional DBMS in all dimensions
questions.explanation:
The rise of NoSQL, NewSQL, and other modern databases is driven by specific limitations of traditional DBMS: scalability issues (can't handle big data growth), rigid schema (can't handle unstructured data), complexity with distributed data (globalisation demand), limited real-time analytics (OLAP weakness), and inability to handle NoSQL requirements. Modern systems address these specific gaps — not replace traditional DBMS entirely.

{"A":"Traditional DBMS are not inherently insecure or buggy — they have specific architectural limitations for modern use cases.","B":"Cost is one factor but not the primary driver — architectural limitations are the core cause.","C":"✓ Correct — specific technical limitations (scale, schema, distribution, analytics, NoSQL data) drove modern database innovation.","D":"NoSQL is better for certain use cases — but traditional DBMS remain superior for structured transactional data."}

questions.text:
Two different organisations have the same budget and the same scale. Organisation A: user data is structured (fixed schema), all operations are short transactions (debit, credit, transfer), and regulatory compliance requires ACID guarantees. Organisation B: user data is semi-structured (social posts, images, comments), queries are exploratory and analytical, and scale must grow 10x in 6 months.

Which database types should Organisations A and B respectively choose, and why?
opts: A: NoSQL; B: RDBMS — NoSQL is always faster; RDBMS is always more flexible
A: RDBMS — structured data + ACID + transactional = relational model; B: NoSQL — semi-structured + analytical + rapid scale = NoSQL document/column store
A: Time-Series; B: Graph — all modern applications need specialised databases
A: Distributed; B: Cloud — distribution and cloud always outperform traditional DBMS
questions.explanation:
Organisation A: structured, transactional, ACID-required = RDBMS is the clear match. Organisation B: semi-structured social data (document store), analytical (column-family store), rapid 10x scaling (NoSQL horizontal scaling) = NoSQL. This illustrates the core database selection principle: match the data model and workload type to the database type. Budget and scale alone do not determine the choice.

{"A":"NoSQL is not always faster and RDBMS is not always more flexible — each fits different use cases.","B":"✓ Correct — structured+ACID+transactional → RDBMS; semi-structured+analytical+rapid scale → NoSQL.","C":"Time-Series and Graph are specialised for specific domains — not general replacements for transactional or social media systems.","D":"Distribution and cloud are deployment and scaling strategies — not the primary selection criteria between data models."}

questions.text:
A final exam question asks students to evaluate: "A ride-hailing company needs to: (1) store fixed-format trip records with ACID guarantees; (2) match drivers and riders in real-time using location and preference graph data; (3) analyse hourly ride demand trends across Lagos by time of day; (4) serve user profile lookups at 1 million queries per second."

Which combination of database types best serves all four requirements?
opts: (1) RDBMS, (2) Graph Database, (3) Time-Series Database, (4) Key-Value Store
(1) NoSQL Document Store, (2) Relational Database, (3) Key-Value Store, (4) Graph Database
(1) Time-Series Database, (2) Key-Value Store, (3) Relational Database, (4) Graph Database
(1) Hierarchical Database, (2) Network Database, (3) Column-Family Store, (4) Object-Oriented Database
questions.explanation:
(1) Fixed-format trip records + ACID = RDBMS. (2) Real-time driver-rider matching using location/preference relationships = Graph Database (relationship traversal). (3) Time-based demand trends across hours and locations = Time-Series Database (time-indexed analytics). (4) 1M user profile lookups/second by user ID = Key-Value Store (extremely fast single-key lookup). This combination reflects Polyglot Persistence — each database chosen for its domain strength.

{"A":"✓ Correct — RDBMS(trips) + Graph(matching) + TSDB(demand analytics) + Key-Value(profile lookups) = optimal polyglot solution.","B":"This misassigns relational and document stores and puts Key-Value where TSDB is needed.","C":"TSDB for fixed ACID records and Key-Value for matching/routing are mismatches.","D":"Hierarchical and Network databases are legacy models unsuitable for modern real-time applications at this scale."}
